messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus is a 55-year-old divorced fashion designer of Canadian descent who presented for psychological assessment following what he described, with considerable difficulty, as a gradual collapse of his ability to function both professionally and personally. He came to the first session dressed with careful precision, speaking in measured sentences, and only occasionally allowing silences to stretch long enough that the discomfort in his face became visible. The story he eventually told was not a single, dateable event but a sustained childhood landscape of violence at the hands of his father — a man whose moods governed every room he entered, and whose hands were the primary instrument of discipline, correction, and rage. Marcus described years of beatings that were unpredictable in their timing but entirely predictable in their logic: silence in the house often preceded them. His father would go quiet, the television would be switched off, footsteps would slow, and Marcus would know, with the certainty of a child who has learned to read threat the way others read weather, that something was coming. He did not always know what he had done wrong. Sometimes he was told; sometimes he was not. What he carried forward from those years was not a single scene but a whole grammar of danger — one that his nervous system has never stopped speaking.

For most of his adult life, Marcus managed. He built a career in fashion that rewarded his eye for detail and his capacity to work long, solitary hours. His marriage ended in his early forties, and he has lived alone since then. He has always been, by his own account, someone who keeps people at a measured distance — not unfriendly, but careful. He told the intake clinician that he has spent decades believing that people, given enough time and proximity, will eventually reveal themselves to be untrustworthy. This was not a new belief. It was one he had tested quietly across friendships, professional relationships, and his marriage, and found consistently confirmed, at least in his interpretation of events.

What changed in the past two years is harder to locate precisely. Marcus describes a kind of accumulation — a threshold crossed without announcement. He began waking from nightmares and reorganising his evenings in response: he stopped going to bed before midnight, avoided napping, and gave up the long baths he used to take on Sunday evenings because the stillness and warmth had begun to reliably precede disturbing sleep. At work, where he manages a small atelier with two junior designers and a seamstress, he found himself flinching when a colleague touched his shoulder to get his attention over a cutting table. He would recover quickly, laugh it off, but the alarm was real and physical — a full-body jolt that left him embarrassed and watchful. He began positioning himself near doorways during team meetings. The atelier, which had always been a place of controlled creative noise, now felt different to him during quiet periods between collections. When the studio fell silent — no machines, no music, no conversation — Marcus found himself scanning, waiting, certain without any rational basis that the silence contained a threat he had not yet identified.

At home the vigilance intensified. He told the clinician that he checks the locks twice before sitting down in the evening, not because he fears intruders in any articulable way, but because the feeling of being unsafe inside his own apartment has become persistent and sourceless. When he tries to remember specific incidents from his childhood in order to make sense of any of this, he finds the memories arrive either stripped of feeling — as though he is reading a case file about someone else — or accompanied by a wave of guilt so acute that he stops trying. He cannot construct a coherent account of what happened to him; the story has no clean beginning, middle, or end, only fragments and the emotional residue of fragments.

What frightened Marcus most, and what finally brought him to seek help, was his growing conviction that he had been permanently altered — that whatever the person he might have been was, he had been replaced by someone irreparably damaged. He has begun to wonder, with genuine fear rather than metaphor, whether his reactions mean that his mind is no longer functioning as it should. He arrived hoping, in his own words, to understand what is happening to him. He is not sure he believes it can be changed.
